core.text: For *longest, bravest, most beautiful* Latin adds *-issimus -a -um* to the adjective's stem: **the superlative (the '-est / most' form)**. *longus* (long) → *longissimus*; *brevis* (short) → *brevissimus*; *clārus* (bright) → *clārissima stēlla*. Adjectives in *-er* double the *r* instead: *pulcher* → *pulcherrimus*, *piger* (lazy) → *pigerrimus*. The result is an ordinary *-us -a -um* adjective. The group it is the best *of* goes in the genitive (the 'of' form) or after *ex*: *mēnsis annī brevissimus* — the shortest month of the year. Latin name: gradus superlātīvus.
The superlative is the *-est* or *most* form: *tallest, most careful*. It sets one thing against all the rest of its group: *the tallest of the boys*.
Stem + -issimus (-er adjectives: -errimus), declined like bonus; 'of all' = genitive or ex + ablative.

invented.en: Rome is the most beautiful city.

core.text: *-ior* = *more*, two things; *-issimus* = *most*, one against all. *Sōl clārior est quam lūna* — brighter than the moon; *sōl stēlla clārissima est* — the brightest star. The comparative (the '-er / more' form) takes 3rd-declension endings (*clāriōrem*), the superlative *-us -a -um* endings (*clārissimum*), so the ending tells you which one you have.

teach.title: What it does
teach.say: Set one thing against the whole group it belongs to and Latin marks the adjective again: **the superlative (the '-est / most' form)**. *clārus* (bright) → *clārissima stēlla*, the brightest star; *fortis* → *mīles fortissimus*, the bravest soldier. It can also mean simply 'very': *aegerrimus*, very sick indeed.

check.ask: Which word is the superlative, and what has been added to the stem to make it?

teach.title: How it is built: stem + -issimus
teach.say: One cell. Take the stem — the part left when the dictionary ending comes off — and add *-issimus*: *long-* → *longissimus*, *fort-* → *fortissimus*, *clār-* → *clārissimus*. Two *s*'s, then *-imus*.

show.say: longissimus — the stem long- with -issimus on it

check.ask: Give the superlative subject form of *longus*.

teach.title: It declines like bonus -a -um
teach.say: Two cells more. Once built, a superlative is an ordinary 1st/2nd declension adjective: feminine *-issima* (*laetissima*), neuter *-issimum* (*altissimum*), object *-issimum* / *-issimam*, plural *-issimī*, *-issimae*, *-issima*. No new endings at all.

show.say: longissima / longissimum — ordinary -a and -um endings on the superlative stem

check.ask: Now the feminine and the neuter of *longissimus*.

teach.title: Adjectives in -er double the r
teach.say: One group breaks the pattern. An adjective whose masculine ends in *-er* does not take *-issimus*: it doubles the *r* and adds *-imus*. *pulcher* → *pulcherrimus*, *aeger* → *aegerrimus*, *niger* → *nigerrimus*. The endings after that are the same *-us -a -um* ones.

check.ask: Quīntus ___ est, sed Mārcus sānus. *aeger* ends in *-er*, so double the r. (aeger)

teach.title: Telling it from the comparative
teach.say: *-ior* is the comparative (the '-er / more' form) and sets two things side by side; *-issimus* is the superlative and sets one against all the rest. The endings part them too: *fortior* declines like a 3rd-declension noun (*fortiōrem*), *fortissimus* like *bonus* (*fortissimum*).

check.ask: One of *brevior* and *brevissimus* sets two months side by side, the other sets one month against all the rest. Which is which?

teach.title: Using it: naming the group
teach.say: To say what the thing is best of, Latin uses the genitive (the 'of' form) of the group — *fortissimus puerōrum*, the bravest of the boys — or *ex* with the ablative: *altissimus ex puerīs*. Both are ordinary; pick either.

check.ask: Quīntus fortissimus ___ Rōmānōrum est. The group goes into the genitive (the 'of' form). (puer, more than one)

more.text: Six adjectives in *-ilis* use *-limus*: *facilis* → *facillimus* (easiest), *difficilis* → *difficillimus*, *similis* → *simillimus*. Adjectives in *-eus / -ius* say *maximē* (most) instead: *maximē idōneus*.

The superlative often just means *very*: *Aemilia laetissima erat* — Aemilia was very happy. *quam* + superlative means *as … as possible*: *quam celerrimē* — as quickly as possible. As a noun, *-issimī* with a genitive picks out the top of a group: *fortissimus omnium* — the bravest of all.

The learner's notes (week 13): add *-issim-* and then the *-us -a -um* ending (*īnfirmissimus, clāmōsissima, plēnissimum*); *-er* adjectives add *-rim-* to the nominative masculine singular (*pigerrimus, pulcherrima*); the group of comparison is a genitive or *ex* + ablative (*īnfirmissimus omnium*, *plēnissimum ex pōculīs*). Ørberg (chapter XIII): *altissimus, longissima, brevissimum* are superlatives, adjectives of the 1st and 2nd declension; *Aetna mōns Siciliae altissimus est*.
